title: Negotiating With Team Members Looking to Leave
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece examines the risks of negotiating counteroffers with team members who've received outside job offers, arguing the practice can quietly create a 'counteroffer terrorism' dynamic across the whole team. It explains how team members learn, through informal channels, that leaving is a faster route to advancement than staying and earning it, even when deals are supposedly confidential. The article acknowledges some team members are valuable enough to fight for, but insists the decision must weigh long-term team-wide consequences. It closes by placing responsibility for this dynamic on leaders, not on the team members who exploit it.
points: Negotiating counteroffers with departing team members can create a team-wide 'counteroffer terrorism' dynamic.
Team members learn through informal channels that leaving is a faster path to advancement than staying.
Confidentiality around a negotiated deal rarely holds up in practice.
Most team members with an outside offer leave anyway unless the counteroffer is unusually large.
The article places responsibility for this dynamic on leaders' choices, not on team members who exploit it.
quotes: Beyond appealing to their loyalty to their colleagues and their place in the future of the team, leaders typically have several incentives at their disposal to retain a valued team member.
After this pattern repeats itself with several team members over time, leaders unintentionally create a terrorist mindset within the team.
Team members quickly learn that to get more, they must threaten to leave.
In the end, most team members with an offer will leave anyway, unless the bid to retain them is massive.
Counteroffer terrorism is created in organizations by leaders, not by team members.
